title: Taking Email to Task: The Design and Evaluation of a Task Management Centered Email Tool
research_question: Can redesigning email around task-management activities, threaded task contexts, task metadata, and overview mechanisms better support users who manage work through email?
methodology: The work began with a multi-phase field study of email task management involving 11 Outlook or Eudora users; for seven participants, two to three weeks of filtered incoming and outgoing email were manually analyzed, supplemented by observations, video-recorded triage, and follow-up interviews. Those observations informed the Taskmaster prototype, an Outlook/Exchange add-on that organized messages and related content into task-centered collections called thrasks and added deadlines, reminders, action indicators, and overview mechanisms. Nine participants then used the prototype with live email, with a planned two-week deployment followed by recorded use, structured debriefing, Likert ratings, and free-form explanations.

key_findings.finding: Organizing email and related material into threaded, task-centric collections was well received and helped preserve the context of ongoing work.
Participants rated organizing and deleting content within the thrask model at an average of 4.2 on a five-point love-to-hate scale oriented so that 5 represented strong approval.
Deadlines, reminders, and action indicators were among the more successful task-centric metadata features, receiving ratings around four and helping users track obligations and dependencies.
key_findings.section: Findings — Task-centric Meta-information for All Items

key_findings.finding: Warning-bar aggregation helped users identify which task collection contained the most urgent item and therefore supported prioritization.
Action indicators conveyed that work remained to be done but did not adequately communicate the relative importance of different actions, limiting their usefulness for planning.

Despite substantial prototype instability and missing standard email features, three of the five participants who completed the study did not want to return to Outlook, and three participants were still using Taskmaster four months later.
The authors conclude that embedding task-management resources directly in email can materially improve the experience of managing work through the inbox.

limitations: The prototype evaluation involved only nine users.
Four of the nine evaluation participants did not complete the planned full two-week deployment.
Taskmaster had substantial technical instability, configuration dependencies, and missing standard features such as printing and some addressing functionality.
The study was not a controlled comparison against a mature task-management email system and relied substantially on qualitative observations and participant ratings.
The prototype's metadata and aggregation mechanisms did not adequately represent relative action importance, an explicit limitation for prioritization.
The system organized tasks and reminders but did not formally model resolved, superseded, uncertain, or omitted work-item states across repeated briefing cycles.
raw_claims: Email was functioning as a repository for tasks, ongoing correspondence, and items whose status was not yet determined.
The researchers studied real email activity before designing Taskmaster.
Taskmaster grouped messages, attachments, links, and other related content into task-centered collections.
The prototype exposed deadlines, reminders, action indicators, and other task metadata directly alongside email content.
Nine users participated in the live prototype evaluation.
Seven participants used Taskmaster for at least one full week.
Three participants were still using the prototype four months after the formal study ended.
Users valued seeing newly arrived messages in the context of the surrounding task conversation.
Reminder and deadline features helped some users keep track of actions they owed to other people or were awaiting from others.
Urgency aggregation helped prioritize work, whereas generic action indicators did not show which pending actions mattered most.
Technical problems and missing conventional email features were major causes of early abandonment.
